Entertainment.title: Julia Garner Would Rather Be Someone Else
Entertainment.text:
Julia Garner doesn’t like to think of what she does as acting, not once the cameras are rolling. “I’m just being at that moment,” she said. “I’m just living it.”

She knows how that sounds. “Super artsy,” she said. “Actory.” She can’t help it. “I always want to act and feel like no one is watching me,” she said.

In life, Garner, 32, doesn’t hide. I’d met up with her at Zitomer’s, a multilevel pharmacy on Manhattan’s Upper East Side. This was Garner’s suggestion. She’s been a regular since her high school days, and the salesladies swarmed her. “Hi, honey!” one cooed as Garner swept in.

Garner, pointed out a peel she loves, the first grown-up lipstick she bought, then moved onto blinged-out pill cases, bed jackets and furry Russian hats.

She insisted that I try out a moisturizer with the horrifying name of CelluMoist, and because Garner is sweetly indomitable, I submitted, letting a clerk slather it on. Minutes later I had to wrestle a makeup bag out of Garner’s hand, explaining that our ethics policy prevented her buying it for me. I won. Barely. To be around her, at least on that late summer afternoon, was to be swept up in a very benevolent whirlwind — a twister of zip and warmth and sharp acuity.

I hadn’t expected this. Though Garner’s body of work (“The Americans,” “Ozark,” “The Assistant,” “Weapons”) is unusually varied, none of it implies that she would be a fun hang. But Garner is a transformational actress. By method and by choice she is nothing like the characters she plays.

“When somebody comes along like Julia, who’s beautiful and talented and daring in the way that she is, it feels important,” said Zach Cregger, who directed her in “Weapons,” the buzzy 2025 horror hit. “She just throws herself into all these different roles and is unrecognizable.”

Even out of roles, Garner doesn’t always recognize herself. To me, she seemed distinct, delightfully sui generis. But maybe that was only the Julia of that day, that hour.

Her latest transformation is in “The Altruists,” a Netflix limited series that premieres on Nov. 19. Created by Graham Moore, “The Altruists” describes the spectacular rise and precipitous fall of FTX and Alameda Research, cryptocurrency concerns founded by Sam Bankman-Fried. Garner plays Caroline Ellison, the chief executive of Alameda Research and Bankman-Fried’s off-again-on-again romantic partner. Their relationship — amatory, professional — is depicted as a blockchain folie à deux that ends with both of them imprisoned for crimes including fraud and conspiracy.

You would not think that a person like Garner could disguise her looks easily. With her milky skin, sharp chin, liquid eyes and meringue-like blond curls, she has a delicate, distinct elegance. But the first time Anthony Boyle, who plays Bankman-Fried, saw her fully made up, he mistook her for a background actor.

“It was like a magic trick,” he said. “She was a different person.”

That magic, that sense of not acting but being, is the goal. “I like to become different people,” Garner said. “I am really just trying to completely disappear.”

Early on, she went out for teen and tween parts on Nickelodeon series, but she did not get them. Her look and affect were better suited to indies. She had a significant role in the 2011 cult drama “Martha Marcy May Marlene” and a starring one in “Electrick Children,” a coming-of-age film from 2012. Studio executives encouraged her to dye her hair and get veneers, but she resisted.

“I was like, they have no taste,” she recalled.

She entered the mature phase of her career a few years later on the FX series “The Americans,” playing an C.I.A. officer’s daughter, and was a standout on the Netflix rural crime show “Ozark,” as a baby-faced, dirty-mouthed criminal matriarch.

In these roles and elsewhere, there was a sense of risk in her performances, a heightened emotional intensity or an uncanny remove. Garner described herself as drawn to extremes.

“If I read something and I’m not scared to do it, I just don’t do it,” she said.

She also lends her characters a sense of unpredictability, an aliveness, which she ascribes in part to her experience of childhood epilepsy, never knowing when the next seizure would come. “There is something about that that forces you to be present,” she said.

Garner has an unusual approach to acting. When preparing a role, she invites a character in. “I literally can physically feel when I’m leaving and having another person coming,” she said. “It sounds so crazy.”

The character of Caroline came in from pretty far away. Ellison was a math prodigy; Garner failed math. Ellison is emotionally illiterate; Garner is an emotional whiz. They look nothing alike. But Garner saw “The Altruists” as an opportunity for complete transformation.

“I just wanted to see how far I could go,” she said.

This was why Moore wanted her, too. “Julia is such a high diver,” he said. “She will choose to jump from the highest platform into the deepest water.” Even he was surprised at Garner’s push for physical transformation — colored contacts, facial prosthetics, a wig system, which meant more than two hours each day in the makeup trailer.

Unlike Anna Sorokin, whom Garner played in the Netflix series “Inventing Anna,” Ellison declined a request to meet. From the few videos of her available, Garner roughed out a gawky walk and a gasping laugh. She moved her voice to a lower register, frayed at the ends, and accelerated her speech.

Boyle, acting opposite her, admired her ability to combine this immersion in the role with the practicality a shoot demands. “She treads that line of being able to call on genius and be possessed by it at will and also be in reality,” he said.

“I have to make sure to feed my soul, as corny as that sounds,” she said. “Feed my soul as a human. Because I don’t play actresses, I play people.”

I realized only later, playing back the interview, that she had said almost nothing about that offscreen human. She hadn’t seemed evasive at the time. (Of her separation from her husband, the musician Mark Foster, she said simply, “There’s nothing really to talk about.”) And yet her most personal details were about moisturizer. Just now she seems to live for her work. And there’s plenty of it.

She has recently finished filming “Tyrant,” a suspense movie set in the world of fine dining, co-starring Charlize Theron. Garner will next play one half of an adulterous couple in another thriller, “Guilty Creatures.” She has also shot an episode of the Apple TV Hollywood satire “The Studio,” in which she plays “a crazy version of myself,” opposite Madonna. (Garner was cast as Madonna in a biopic, which remains mired in development.)

I was reminded of something Moore had said, that if you tried to draw a through line linking Garner’s various roles, you would end up with a series of cartoon squiggles. But “The Studio” aside, she has almost never played a character who is happy or at ease or has even half the exuberance and impishness that she displayed that afternoon.

Entertainment.title: How Peter Farrelly Captured a New Side of ‘Rocky’
Entertainment.text:
In “Anatomy of a Scene,” we ask directors to reveal the secrets that go into making key scenes in their movies. See new episodes in the series on Fridays. You can also watch our collection of more than 350 videos on YouTube and subscribe to our YouTube channel.

The movie “I Play Rocky" charts the long and obstacle-hurtling path that Sylvester Stallone took to getting the movie “Rocky” to the big screen. Directed by Peter Farrelly, the movie structures its making-of-“Rocky” narrative in the same triumphant underdog way that the director of “Rocky” structured the original.

This sequence takes place during the shooting of a dramatic sequence in “Rocky.” Anthony Ippolito portrays Sylvester Stallone as he is playing Rocky. And Robert Morgan portrays Burgess Meredith as he is playing Mickey, a trainer, former boxer and the owner of the gym Rocky frequents. In the sequence, after Rocky has been picked to face the heavyweight champion of the world, Apollo Creed, for a chance at the title, Mickey offers to be Rocky’s manager. But Rocky sends him away because he believes Mickey never cared about his potential during the many years he’d been training there.

But in the scene as originally written, Rocky immediately chases after Mickey, without a sense of what might have motivated him to do so. During the shoot, the director of “Rocky,” John G. Avildsen (played by Jay Duplass), feels that the scene is not making sense because he doesn’t understand why Rocky would go after Mickey when Mickey has been critical of Rocky’s talent until now. He challenges Stallone to devise a way to make the sequence come together emotionally.

Stallone takes a break and has a conversation with his wife, Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb). She pushes him to think about why he wrote the scene, and who in his real life never gave him a chance to succeed. With his dismissive father in his head, Stallone returns to the set to shoot the scene, ad-libbing a monologue that feels like an outpouring of his anger over how he’s been treated.

It’s not a scene that most people discuss when talking about “Rocky” (the training montage is usually at the top of the list), but in an interview, Farrelly said, “This is gonna be the scene that people most remember in ‘I Play Rocky.’”

It’s a turning point in the movie, one that zeros in on the many obstructions that have impeded Stallone as he is trying to star in his first movie, the studio skeptical that he will be able to make it work, or that his performance will be up to par. But he transcends those negative thoughts in this moment, wowing both his director and his producers on the set.

Entertainment.title: Offset Is Tired of Being Rap’s Bad Guy: ‘I Got Lost’
Entertainment.text:
Modern rap stardom can be both musical and extramusical. Offset, who came to fame as a member of the superstar Atlanta rap trio Migos, alongside Quavo and Takeoff, has had a heavy dose of each.

Born Kiari Cephus, Offset, 34, was one of the artists who remade the sound of hip-hop at the dawn of streaming in the 2010s, helping cement Atlanta as a center of rap innovation and success. Following the group’s early hits like “Versace” and “Fight Night,” which established their trademark flow through percussive repetition, Offset differentiated himself by writing the hook for “Bad and Boujee,” one of the decade’s defining rap songs and an unlikely Billboard No. 1.

But he was also the Migos member with the most fraught personal life: As the trio celebrated early triumphs, he was in and out of jail, facing a tangle of charges stemming from a youthful conviction for burglary.

Over the last few years, Offset has become as visible for his personal foibles and setbacks as his musicmaking. His marriage to, and split from, Cardi B provided years of tabloid fodder, making him a regular and reliable villain of the social internet. Earlier this year, he was shot outside a Florida casino. And he’s still living under the long shadow cast by the 2022 fatal shooting of Takeoff — a close friend from adolescence whom he continues to refer to as a brother — which occurred while Offset was suing Migos’s label and estranged from the group.

JOE COSCARELLI Let’s start with the title track, “GMFU.” This is the place you put years of angst, everything you’ve been through recently — Takeoff’s death, your own shooting, your marriage collapsing. What was your mind-set going into recording a clearing-the-air song, and how does it differ from the mind-set that you’re in now?

OFFSET I got lost. I went through so many hits, and I feel like it became a blur to what my passion is, which is music, you know? The personal takes went so far on things that have happened in my life that I’ve taken full accountability of before, and it’s like, sometimes I can’t escape the matrix of this narrative. And so when I made this album, I got in a bag where I was like, you know what, I’m going to just focus on this music. I don’t really hear all the noise. I am a great person. I know this. I have Black women around me that know I’m a great man at the end of the day: my mother, my creative director-slash-manager. And I got children that I look out for, that I’m a great father to. And sometimes other things blur that, and it bothers me.

Because you got to understand, when I first started, I was the knucklehead in the group. I was going to jail. I ain’t been to jail in over 10 years. I straightened that, and it was so hard to stray from that to become a professional. And to grow up. My music is my pulse, my heart. That’s all I have. And so I wasn’t treating it that way, because of all the other things that was happening. I went into the dark space, gambling. When I gambled, it’s just like, OK, this is just about this — I don’t have to see no tabloids or worry about somebody saying something about me. It blinds you as if it’s not an issue, and it really is an issue.

COSCARELLI This villain narrative out there — is it because of your personal life?

OFFSET Yeah, it’s the past relationship. What’s so crazy is we good — me and her good. It was a patch of time that happened. We have children. We see the bigger thing. Me and her cool. But it’s more the people, you know what I’m saying, more than what’s actually happened in real life. Like, I have no issues with my ex. I salute everything that she’s doing.

JON CARAMANICA But that doesn’t travel as well on the internet as when you’re not good. People are obviously going to amplify the negative. Are you trying to be proactive to demonstrate that things are good now?

CARAMANICA Do you think that the things that people get frustrated with or talk about online — your villain narrative — are the same things that you experienced as you were lost, or is it two totally separate things?

OFFSET Uhhhh, they go together, ’cause I was doing lost [expletive], publicly. So it’s kind of on me. It’s not kind of — it’s on me.

COSCARELLI Was there any side of you that was like, you know what, they have a point?

OFFSET A million percent. Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.

CARAMANICA Was that hard to look at — like, these are strangers on the internet, and they can see that I’m not doing right?

OFFSET It wasn’t so tough when you’ve got a strong mama who’s going to tell you what it is.

Sometimes it takes for somebody at home to shake you up, like, hey, what you doing? And then I can sometimes see the hurt in my mama. And that burns my soul, bro. Burns my soul. I’ve been trying to change for my family’s sake, and then sometimes it don’t go nowhere. I don’t know what to do a lot of times, but I do have to acknowledge that I brought all this [expletive] on myself. I went through dark times.

COSCARELLI Your marriage is imploding.

OFFSET My brother died.

COSCARELLI Takeoff died, of course, in this same stretch. And then you have this incident at a casino. You got shot. There’s these photos of you in the hospital — you’re smoking a cigarette in a wheelchair, and your mom is with you. She looks like she’s —

OFFSET She’s getting on my ass. She ain’t playing, because I broke my mama’s heart, bro. I ain’t never seen my mama like that.

COSCARELLI Even with all you’ve been through?

OFFSET All I’ve been through, that was a different moment. Like, my mama eyes — like, her baby boy. You know, when I got hit, I called my mama, so she wouldn’t hear it from the street. You know, “I’m good, I just got to go to the hospital” — hung up. Actually, my phone died, which was worse. She flew in so fast. When I was outside, I’m talking to her — really, I wanted to get up out of there — but she gave it to me: You being a coward to your kids by making choices like this that’s affecting everybody. You could be dead. You know, she gave me the talk. You the savior to the family. What you doing? But it wasn’t that nice, you know what I mean? It wasn’t nice. My mama hold me accountable. She’s worried, but it was more like, you need discipline.

COSCARELLI How do you start to build yourself back up?

OFFSET When I was saying lost, I was not moving as Offset, because I didn’t want to be Offset at one point. Because it was just too much. It’s like, working hard to become an artist, and then your relationship smokes that whole [expletive]. And I ain’t playing no victim, though. I don’t want to play no victim. I don’t want people to see this and be like, are you playing a victim? I’m just saying, I’m tired of that.

COSCARELLI What did you have to change lifestyle-wise, post-shooting, to make sure you could be Offset again?

OFFSET At that time, I wasn’t even recording. I was literally trying to get away from folks. I wasn’t trying to go to no club, no strip club. I just was sitting around. I just want to be Kiari. I was trying to get back to the person, to be present. Because the opposite person ain’t working.

COSCARELLI Do you feel like you have a problem with gambling?

OFFSET I don’t know. I’m going to be a million percent real with y’all. I like to gamble, right? I feel like I need to stop. I need to stop. But I feel like a problem is when you, like, selling [expletive], you ain’t got the money to do it. I’m doing this [expletive] to get away. And I do like to gamble, to be honest. A lot of plays I get, you think I’m gambling, and I’ve been paid a lot of money to maybe promote it.

CARAMANICA Like from gambling platforms?

OFFSET Yeah, so I might have a sponsorship from them. They have a lot of budget. Sometimes you think I’m gambling and I might’ve collabed with somebody, but I just made $400,000 doing this. I’ma keep it real, like — I can say I got a problem. I’m not trying to give myself an excuse, because I sound kind of excuse-y.

CARAMANICA All this music on the new album was recorded after the shooting?

OFFSET All after. Yeah. I went right to the lab. I got out of the hospital, I’m in the studio.

COSCARELLI I remember the same thing happened when you almost died in a car wreck.

OFFSET You make the smashes when you go through stuff and go straight to the studio, ’cause now you got something to talk about. And I started just talking like that. It put me back in the focus mind. And I’m just being honest, you got to distract yourself from that. Because it’s a deep tunnel going into that, and you can’t come back sometimes, you feel me? So I just got to work.

OFFSET I don’t look at it like that. For me, it’s like, I know I’m not Migos. That’s three monsters in one machine, right? So it’s not a frustration for me, it’s a building for me. I got four solo albums out, right? Every album, I caught a single that went to Billboard, right? So I never did a flop album, in my eyes.

Might not have been as peak as Migos, but Migos took 15 years to get to that peak. Y’all just seen it after five or six — we’ve been rappers since eighth grade. So I still remember that it’s a buildup. I feel like a lot of people really get lost in the sauce when they don’t recognize things are changing, bro. You still could be a big artist and in a good position, still make millions every year, but you’re not recognizing the change.

BreakingNewsTab.title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.

The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel, Atlantic Asphalt.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Captain Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort went to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".

"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.

Calls about the collision came in around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans Chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port of New Orleans.

Passengers began disembarking from the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping on to its side, Mayor Moreno said.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help and officials shut down the Mississippi River for the search effort.

The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.

President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue was an "incredible job".

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said the US Coast Guard also supported local rescue operations.

Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.

BreakingNewsTab.title: US Air Force says it responded to 'suspected drones' over RAF Lakenheath
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The US Air Force said it responded to "suspected unauthorised drone activity" over RAF Lakenheath in Suffolk on Friday evening.

No personnel, aircraft or infrastructure were affected, a spokesperson for the US Air Force said.

It comes after unconfirmed reports that sirens were sounded at the base, which residents reported hearing from a nearby village.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson told the BBC it was "coordinating with all relevant parties", adding that US Air Force security personnel responded to the reports and the situation was resolved.

"We are working closely with them to establish the facts," they added.

West Suffolk MP Nick Timothy said he had been in touch with authorities at the base, and was told "there is no threat to the public, and the incident is now resolved".

"Given the raised threat level, I continue to encourage everyone to report anything suspicious or out of the ordinary to the authorities," he added in a social media post.

Earlier this week, at least 12 US Air Force aircraft departed the nearby RAF Mildenhall base.

They included two Boeing Stratotanker KC-135 refuelling aircraft, with one apparently headed towards Germany and another seen landing at Prestwick Airport near Glasgow.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Police investigating David Walliams over reports alleging serious sexual offences
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The Metropolitan Police has launched an investigation into David Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences".

It comes after ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

The Met said that the allegations being investigated are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian, but as "part of their investigation, detectives are also proactively reviewing that reporting to establish whether there is any evidence of offences".

When those allegations were first reported, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

In a statement released on Friday, the Met said it had "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offences involving a man now in his 50s".

"Those who have come forward are being supported by specialist officers," the statement added.

Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney said: "We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offence to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened.

"We know reporting allegations of this nature can be daunting, but specialist officers are on hand to provide support, answer questions and guide you through the process."

Allegations against the entertainer and children's author were published after he lost a legal bid to stop claims against him being made public by the media.

Some of the women in the investigation accused Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.

One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Guardian and ITV News said that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

The investigation also claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret.

"And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

Walliams shot to fame in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation which helped to resolve the Cold War.

The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement which included China, which has been building up its arsenal.

Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could turn up major hurdles and take years.

BreakingNewsTab.title: First catch aborted in SpaceX Starship rocket double-catch test
BreakingNewsTab.text:
SpaceX aborted its attempt to catch the bottom part of its huge Starship rocket during its latest test flight.

The aim was to catch it using the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on the launch tower as it returned to Earth, but instead it was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames as it came down.

The top part of the rocket is now continuing its journey to space, and SpaceX will decide whether it will try to catch this rocket stage at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday.

It is the company's first attempt to fully recover its rocket, paving the way for making Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.

The 124m-tall rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time (22:45 GMT) on Friday.

It was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned to the launch tower, but instead it was diverted to the ocean.

During a stream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority, and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each maneuver safely."

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet from space.

The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted.

SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.

But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead, it has splashed down in the ocean.

Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it is in space.

If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.

Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.

In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.

Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year, and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.

But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society.

"Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.

"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."

After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.

The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.

SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it is not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.

Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.

This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.

Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.

But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.

Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK weather: Frost and freezing fog forecast as cold health alerts continue
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Arctic air will maintain its grip on the UK to start the weekend, as cold health alerts remain in place for a large swathe of England.

Saturday will dawn with another sharp and widespread frost with the coldest conditions expected in England and Wales.

Patches of freezing fog could also be a hazard, reducing visibility and bringing a risk of very slippery surfaces in southern and eastern England.

Then it is all change by Sunday with most areas having a frost-free start, but heavy bursts of rain and brisk winds will sweep across the country later.

Saturday will start with temperatures widely below freezing in parts of England and Wales.

Lows in towns and cities are expected to fall to -2 or -3C, but in the countryside they could be as low as -5C.

In southern and south-east England there could also be some patchy freezing fog which forms in air that is below freezing.

Super-cooled water droplets remain suspended in the air and it can be particularly dangerous as they can freeze on impact turning untreated pavements into instant ice rinks.

Yellow cold health alerts from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) are in force for the West Midlands and north-west England until 12:00 Saturday, external.

More of a breeze further north will mean most places will be a few degrees above freezing.

After the fog and frost clears, Saturday will largely become a bright and dry day.

By the afternoon, temperatures will rise across the UK - ranging from 7C in parts of the Highlands to a milder 12C in south-west England.

England and Wales are forecast to see long spells of sunshine, away from the odd shower early on in the far north-west.

Northern Ireland will have some bright spells in the morning, with thickening cloud in the afternoon and rain by evening.

A few showers are expected in parts of Scotland where is will also be a breezy day, and will feel colder due to the wind chill.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.

That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.

And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?

The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."

Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.

What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.

Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.

What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".

That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.

But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.

"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.

"Our proposals were almost laughed at.

"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."

The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".

"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."

Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.

Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.

This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.

After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.

But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.

"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
BreakingNewsTab.text:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.

Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.

Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".

"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.

Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.

"He definitely feels lonely," he says.

Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., external

Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.

"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."

King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.

"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."

African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.

But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.

In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.

It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.

"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.

"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."

Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.

The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.

And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".

But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.

No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.

Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.

These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.

The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".

The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.

"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.

And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.

"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.

Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."

Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."

But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.

Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.

"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."

That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.

"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.

"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Poundland gets more time to secure a rescue deal as emergency talks continue
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Poundland has avoided immediate collapse after a deadline was extended to find a rescue deal.

A deadline to secure a buyer for the retail chain was set to expire at midnight, but a court has given Poundland an extra 10 days to find a buyer.

The discount chain, which has 11,000 employees, has been edging towards administration after being blocked by owners Gordon Brothers from accessing cash in its bank accounts.

A committee of MPs questioned Gordon Brothers following accusations that the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off Poundland's 600 shops and stock piecemeal.

Gordon Brothers - which bought the chain for just £1 last year - is accused of forcing that outcome by restricting Poundland's access to available cash needed to restock shops, and pay wages and rent, ahead of the crucial Christmas trading period.

The investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claims.

However, pressure remains on Poundland's owners after a takeover bid was rejected. The decision prompted calls for answers from politicians, including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

About £50m had been frozen by Gordon Brothers, the BBC understands, meaning Poundland bosses were unable to restock shelves across its 600 shops.

The BBC understands that Gordon Brothers agreed to release a further £11m today from Poundland's accounts, on top of £10m announced earlier, as the firm seeks to find a new buyer.

Gordon Brothers said it was in talks with three parties for a sale of the whole business, and it had received "several offers from established high street retailers for significant parts of the business".

Following the meeting between MPs on the business and trade committee and representatives of Gordon Brothers, chairman Liam Byrne told the BBC that he was "deeply concerned" and described the firm's behaviour as "much like a wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street".

"They refused to prioritise protecting jobs and stores over and above their own financial returns," he said.

"It's clear that they've taken millions out of Poundland at a time when they themselves said the business was on a knife edge."

Byrne said the committee's message to Gordon Brothers was to ensure Poundland had "access to the funds that it needs to trade at what should be one of the busiest periods in the year".

He urged Gordon Brothers to "do what is right to save jobs and stores and do that now".

"It's a good business, it's a much-loved business and, particularly in the middle of the cost of living crisis, communities up and down the country rely on access to the kind of stores that it operates," Byrne added.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Russell Brand, David Walliams and Married at First Sight: Is this a reckoning for TV?
BreakingNewsTab.text:
This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.

On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.

By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.

Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.

These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.

So why is this all happening now?

In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.

All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.

"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.

In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.

Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.

It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".

When looking at what’s driving more women to speak up, much can be traced back to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement.

It changed the perception of whether victims would be believed.

In the past, women alleging this sort of behaviour faced barriers - being seen as opportunistic, fearing retaliation, believing they might be the only one.

Now, there can be a snowball effect. Once one, two or three come forward, that prompts others to revisit their experiences - which they may have dismissed or subdued.

"There is more of a sense that you will now be listened to," said Freeman.

It's also clear that when women see action taken, it can encourage others to speak up as well - as it helps counter the widely-held assumption that reporting abuse results in nothing.

When another high-profile man, MasterChef presenter Gregg Wallace, faced accusations of a very different and much lesser order, relating mostly to inappropriate sexual language and humour, the reaction was similar.

Last summer, an independent inquiry upheld dozens of claims against him, and he was sacked. Wallace said "none of the serious allegations" against him had been upheld but that he was "deeply sorry for any distress caused".

One young woman I spoke to in my investigation into Wallace texted me at the time, to give her reaction to his sacking.

"I really believe this will encourage young girls going into the TV industry to have the courage to speak up, if they feel something is wrong," she told me.

But unions say it is still difficult for junior freelance workers, who often find their income unstable and unpredictable, to speak up.

Vulnerable workers "continue to fear raising concerns", said head of broadcast union Bectu, Philippa Childs.

She's echoed by Freeman, who said an "attitude of protecting the talent" remained.

"There will always be wealthy famous predators," she said. But, she added: "Hopefully more and more people at TV stations and movie studios are willing to hear these young people and will take them seriously”.

For more senior people in TV, raising the alarm can also be difficult.

Earlier this week, comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News: "The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work, because you're seen that you might be a trouble causer. It does need to be said that there needs to be some intervention."

Social media has also played a role in encouraging people to speak up.

And policing investigations have had to keep pace - and adapt - with media scrutiny often prompting authorities to investigate.

Attitudes towards women who speak up are also starting to change – although not always.

Some of what unfolded in court during the Russell Brand case felt like a throwback to how rape cases used to be conducted.

Many have commented on Brand's lawyer's defence tactics against the accusers on the stand - behaviour Freeman said would have been "standard" in the past.

But Freeman noted it was heartening to hear the judge’s remarks in summing up the case - which have also been widely shared by women online and praised for dispelling rape myths.

When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Brand to ten-and-a-half years, he told him: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no."

"I think attitudes have changed,” said Freeman. “It doesn't mean those assaults don't happen any more but attitudes around them have changed.”

So where does this go from here?

Events of the past few weeks highlight how figures who rose to prominence in the nineties and noughties did so in an era with different standards.

Lad culture and celebrity status shielded Brand and others from scrutiny.

Now, behaviour once dismissed as eccentricity or womanising is increasingly being reassessed and called out. Times are catching up with some men of that era.

However, it would be an error to assume this sort of behaviour is confined to the past.

"This is not just about nineties/noughties culture," Wark told me. "It can't be dismissed as a hangover of the past, this is about right now and the industry changes that must happen.

"There will be more cases to come, sexual abuse, coercive control, verbal and physical abuse. It is not OK, and it never was OK."

Then there’s the use of gagging orders and other legal routes often used by celebrities and media organisations to stop women speaking out.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected an injunction request by Walliams, clearing the way for him to be named.

"There are lots of barriers to speaking out, and those that have access to wealth or fame will often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from doing so," Harriet Wistrich, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told me.

That too, may be starting to change.

This week, multiple government ministers have spoken against non-disclosure agreements and called for further restrictions on their use.

Change could come in other areas too.

Next week, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will convene industry leaders to urge them to improve safeguarding practices - while Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front an MPs on Tuesday.

When MAFS UK was cancelled, Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code.

There is growing recognition that those at the top of media organisations have a responsibility to root out abuse. It can't just be down to the victims.

"People in positions of power have a duty to speak up too," said Wark.

"Broadcasters, production companies and those financing productions all have a responsibility to ensure protections are upheld," added Josephine Brassey, from Women in Film and TV, while Philippa Childs urged the creative industries to accept that their current internal reporting mechanisms were "inadequate".

What everyone seems to agree on is that this can't be another empty tipping point with no real, lasting change.

Maybe this time it could really be a watershed moment.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Fast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist

The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.

It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland, external last month.

Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."

Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.

The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.

The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.

During her opening night in Brixton, Newman debuted her new song Survival and was also joined by fellow London soul-pop singer Gabrielle for a duet of her 1993 hit Dreams.

Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.

Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.

But after three more gigs this weekend and an extra date next weekend, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.

She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her.

"Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me.

"I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."

She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."

Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC.

"The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted.

"No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill.

"But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."

After more gigs in Brixton, Brighton and Manchester, she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles next month for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked".

"'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request.

"It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zayn were my favourites.

"So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Pope Leo visits the Peruvian city that has embraced him as one of its own
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Pope Leo XIV has celebrated Mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.

The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.

The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.

"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.

"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago.

Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the Mass began.

"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.

Many came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.

Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.

Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional.

The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached.

They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C.

For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight.

"The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.

Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff, who was elected in May 2025.

The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.

The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.

Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.

Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.

But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.

Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.

But for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes.

"It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.

And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela.

"It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country.

"So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."

Normally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.

Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.

But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the Mass.

Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event.

Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff.

"As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

FinanceTab.title: Heat pumps: How much heat does your home really need?
FinanceTab.text:
Floorplans. Air duct diagrams. Heat pump specifications. Most people in the market for a new heating system probably don't want to think about this level of detail.

But, perhaps surprisingly, some do want to think about those things. In extreme depth.

Every day, roughly 150 new users sign up to an app called Cool Calc, which works out the heat requirements of properties in the US.

Just over one third of those new users are not tradespeople but private homeowners, says founder and chief executive Bill Fiore.

When choosing a heating system, people can find themselves bombarded with information – how powerful a heat pump do they need, for example? It isn't always easy to take a tradesperson at their word.

"As an overall trend, we are seeing homeowners be more informed," explains Fiore. "They want to do a calculation on their own."

A heat loss calculation is a figure, usually measured in watts, that defines how much heat a home loses during cold weather. It's worked out room by room and is a key part of designing an efficient heating system.

This estimate is especially important to get right when installing a heat pump, which is sized fairly precisely, according to the projected heat loss.

Should that calculation be off, the heat pump will likely perform poorly. You could be left with an underpowered device that struggles to warm your property, for example. Given the costs involved, homeowners are often anxious to ensure installers avoid such mistakes.

Certain new technologies are not, for the moment, helping, adds Fiore. "People are going to AI and they're getting a lot of misinformation because it's not backed by anything credible," he says. Cool Calc is planning to integrate with AI chatbots to try and improve the quality of the advice they spew out.

It is probably a good idea to be cautious about your new heating system's design, says Kevin Kircher at Purdue University. He and colleagues recently conducted a study, yet to be published, examining the heat loss calculations provided by tradespeople to roughly 75 US homeowners.

"We were surprised," says Kircher. "The heat loss calculations often led to overestimating the design heat loads by a factor of two or more." That would result in oversized systems that use much more power than necessary.

Not only that, some people reported charges of more than $1,000 (£745) – and in one case as much as $2,500 – just for a heat loss survey, adds Kircher.

Besides using excessive amounts of energy, an oversized heating system can also feel uncomfortable, says Dan Dempsey, a former senior engineering fellow for a major heating and cooling provider in the US.

Dempsey, who took part in Kircher and his colleagues' study, lives in Indiana. He says it is his retirement hobby to monitor the performance of heating and cooling systems in the homes of friends and family members, by analysing data from their smart thermostats.

"I spent five years manually downloading everything, every week," he says. He points out that oversized systems tend to cycle a lot, meaning they switch on and off again in quick succession.

This leads to discernible swings in temperature: rooms that fail to remain at their target temperature of, say, 20C, but rather fluctuate, which feels uncomfortable, says Dempsey.

For people seeking a better understanding of their home's heat loss, various free or partially free apps, including Cool Calc and AutoHVAC, are available. There are options for UK homeowners, too, such as web app Heatpunk.

Doing your own heat loss calculation may end up "over-intellectualising" things, says Adam Chapman, chief geek at heat pump training firm and installer network Heat Geek.

"I don't personally see what a homeowner would gain from it," he says. "We will guarantee the efficiency with way less radiators and pipework upgrades than any other system out there."

Chapman points out that only the most careful of surveys will capture a home's heat loss well.

He says it is common for Heat Geek installers to discover retrofitted windows that haven't been foam-insulated into their openings, leaving draughty gaps, or cavity walls that a homeowner thought had been insulated – but which were actually missed by the builder.

"It's stuff you can't see," he says. "What we actually need is home surveys that go and spot for these sorts of things."

FinanceTab.title: Andy Burnham says 'win-win' deal can be agreed between UK and EU
FinanceTab.text:
Andy Burnham said he believes a "win-win" deal can be agreed with the European Union, adding it could be "more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for" in 2016.

The prime minister is exploring closer ties with the bloc and is expected to sign new agreements on food, energy and youth mobility at a UK-EU summit on 20 November.

Speaking after meeting European leaders in Ireland on Thursday, Burnham said he hopes a deal could help lower prices and boost the UK economy. He predicted the negotiations could "go down to the wire".

The Conservatives have previously said Labour are "dragging us into the European Union via the back door with their EU reset".

While Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good", he has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election.

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The manifesto also said the party wanted to "make Brexit work" and reset the UK's relationship with the EU.

Former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer struck a deal in May 2025 covering fishing, trade and other areas and next week's summit will see the UK government seek to agree further changes.

Burnham has also made clear he wants to examine the "pros and cons" of the options for Britain's long-term relationship with the bloc.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Burnham was asked to explain if his decision to reopen the debate on the UK's future with Europe had helped or hindered the negotiations linked to the summit.

Burnham replied "I think it has helped" before adding: "We've got a big week ahead of us to try and get this deal over the line.

"But let's be clear what's at stake: what we can achieve through this deal is lower prices for British consumers, lower costs for British businesses, more growth in our economy so there's really big prizes here, and I will fight now over the days to come to make sure we get this deal over the line."

Pressed on whether discounted university tuition fees for European students would be part of the deal, Burnham said "requests are coming from the European side, we are putting our requests on the table too".

He added: "I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. I think it actually could be more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016."

Ahead of the summit, the UK and EU agreed a draft deal on removing post-Brexit checks from food and agriculture exports.

Similar texts for deals on emissions trading and a youth travel and work scheme have also been circulated to EU nations.

As a result of the agreement, the government claims the UK economy will eventually see £5.1bn worth of annual benefits.

Burnham also told MPs last month that the summit presents an opportunity to make progress on "controlling illegal immigration".

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch has previously strongly opposed any move to align with EU rules, saying it would "actually take us backwards".

On Thursday, Conservative MP and former minister Dame Priti Patel said: "Andy Burnham's obsession with the EU risks dragging Britain backwards, damaging our economy and leaving hardworking British taxpayers footing the bill."

The Liberal Democrats earlier this month described the draft deal as a "patch, not a fix" and said the "real solution is to re-join the single market and to establish a customs union with the EU".

Reform UK believes one of the "key benefits" of Brexit is that Britain no longer has to "adhere to ridiculous EU rules" and any form of alignment could have a negative impact on the country's trade policy.

The Green Party has called for the UK to re-join the customs union, with leader Zack Polanski previously saying "full membership of the EU remains the best option for the UK".

FinanceTab.title: Why the UK economy is surprisingly resilient
FinanceTab.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

"Top gear" and "strikingly strong" were among the descriptions of the 0.7% growth offered by the economists who track every minor murmur of Britain's economy.

It is an upgrade on "solid" and "resilient", and in turn a world away from "hardest hit by the Iran War".

Against the backdrop of the world's biggest disruption to energy flows, rising market borrowing costs - and the cruel summers since the pandemic - it is impressive growth.

It should reset some of the swirl of self-reinforcing negativity.

The UK's economic growth has averaged less than 0.1% in the four Q3s [ie July to September] since the pandemic.

The average prediction just months ago for this July to September was just 0.1%.

Even the UK's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) effectively pencilled in 0.3% at the Budget just 3 weeks ago.

This figure has not been exceeded outside the pandemic since 2017. It puts the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy after the US across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.

It is tempting to think about what the economy would have done if the Iran War hadn't happened. If interest rates had been cut instead of their recent rise.

While the latest figure kills the doom, it is clearly not a boom either.

Spending on AI and tech have driven the surprise upside over the year. While the AI data centre boom may at any point turn to bust, these figures suggest that spending across the economy on investing in these technologies is helping to boost growth. Consumers have been resilient, at least till the autumn, perhaps helped by better economic vibes.

While there has been an understandable focus on high UK borrowing costs, another measure of the international standing of the UK economy, sterling's value, reached post Brexit referendum highs last week.

Productivity and investment is also looking stronger, especially after recent revisions. Some of the most encouraging figures are in private sector business investment.

I spoke to the chancellor at Nexeon in Oxfordshire, which is searching for a UK factory to manufacture its cutting edge electric vehicle battery - and British - technology. My colleagues visited British watchmakers in Maidenhead carving out a niche to take on the Swiss.

However, this may well not last for the final three months of the year.

Consumer confidence has already fallen as petrol and domestic energy prices start to rise again.

There is a significant challenge with everyday cost-of-living pressures in the coming months. Construction and private house building remain depressed.

The Iran conflict remains the big unknown and whether post the US midterm elections there could be a durable end to the conflict in the Gulf.

Some oil and gas production there is starting to normalise. It could bring down petrol prices, energy bills, government borrowing costs, and mortgage costs too.

Expect to see Downing Street investing heavily in "settlement of the conflict", which the chancellor told me is the "best economic policy".

FinanceTab.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
FinanceTab.text:
The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.

Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the previous three months, official figures, external show.

The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.

Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by cloud computing and AI-linked spending.

The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.

Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.

But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.

However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".

"Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future," he said.

Chancellor John Healey told the BBC the figures showed a "remarkable resilience" in the face of global conflicts, and hopes they "bring back confidence in Britain".

Asked about how government decisions could be the reason for growth when AI investment has been a main driver, Healey said ministers can always "help or hinder" business confidence and investments.
